bib.title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work-Until They Don't

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't". Zhiyuan Jiang (Princeton; equal-contribution first author, work done as intern), Fangrui Huang (Stanford), Hanwen Xing (USC), Xander Wu (Stanford), Yipeng Gao (USC), Rui Cao (Johns Hopkins), Mengdi Wang (Princeton), Shilong Liu (Princeton), Yijiang Li (UC San Diego). The last three are corresponding authors. arXiv:2608.14036v1 [cs.AI], 14 Aug 2026. Marked "*Preprint", no venue.

COVERAGE: All 28 pages and 105,695 chars were read. This includes the appendices (A.1-A.9) and the prompts in Appendix B. I skimmed the references, and the tail of the prompt section only lightly. Appendix Tables 15 and 16 (full recall/F1 and no-hint numbers) were referenced but not seen in the extraction. Figures 2-5 were not viewed. I took the numbers from the text and from Tables 1, 4, 9-13.

MAIN CLAIM: Skills help mainly as "procedural anchors" that stabilise execution. They do not mostly inject missing facts. Their gains over raw execution are small and uncertain. Their clearest gain is over workflow memory built from the same trajectories. Retrieval and invocation are a separate failure point.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Skill vs Workflow Memory, with the same source trajectories.
   - Setup: Codex + GPT-5.3-Codex and Gemini CLI + Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview. Benchmarks are Terminal-Bench 2.0, SkillsBench and Terminal-Bench-Pro. There are 528 paired task triples, using one representative trial per arm.
   - Oracle success rates (Table 9): skill 327/528 = 61.9%, raw 312/528 = 59.1%, workflow 295/528 = 55.9%.
   - Skill vs workflow is +6.06 points (95% bootstrap CI [+0.76, +11.36]).
   - Skill vs raw is +2.84 points, with a CI that spans zero ([-2.27, +7.95]).
2. Mechanism labels, assigned by an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6).
   - Procedural anchoring accounts for 65.7% of skill cases. Knowledge injection accounts for 4.5%.
   - Skill-arm "guidance misapplied or ignored" is 10.0%, against 0.8% for raw.
   - Timeout/budget exhaustion is 10.6% for workflow memory, against 4.4% for skill and 1.7% for raw.
3. Retrieval on SkillsBench (RQ4).
   - Setup: Gemini CLI + Gemini-3.1-Pro and Codex + GPT-5.4. Pool sizes run from 5 to 100. Distractors are random, similar or dissimilar. Arm 3 uses 5 trials per task. The embedding retriever is Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.
   - Actual-use precision falls from 29.6% to 3.3% as the pool grows from 5 to 100. Downstream success stays flat to slightly up, from 36.4% to 39.3%.
   - Offline top-1 embedding precision falls from 88.3% to 76.9%. Explicit agent selection falls from 70.0% to 63.7%.
   - On similar pools, embedding top-1 falls from 70.5% to 53.4%. On random pools it falls from 97.7% to 84.1%. The paper calls semantic confusability the bigger stressor.
4. Compact-text control on 26 Terminal-Bench-2 tasks with Gemini, 5 trials each, 130 trials per condition (Table 12).
   - Skill 79.2%, workflow memory 62.3%, test-first template 59.2%, raw 50.0%, short plan 47.7%.
   - Cross-framework transfer (Fig. 4, read from the figure): skills built from Codex trajectories and run in Gemini CLI beat a 56% raw baseline by +16 to +30 points. I did not verify the workflow-memory side.

Other numbers:
- On an 83-task token-matched set, skill gives +5.5 points over raw. Skill uses 521.5K tokens, workflow memory 426.2K and raw 555.7K.
- Skills cut execution-layer failures (SC2) to 23.5% of labels, from 37.3% for raw.
- Removing the success/failure labels from skill construction hurts once failed trajectories are in the source pool. Gemini on Terminal-Bench-2 at 3s2f scores 0.7462 with labels and 0.4000 without.

QUOTES
- "Skills improve over Workflow Memory by 6.06 points in matched comparisons. Procedural anchoring accounts for 65.7% of skill cases, versus 4.5% for explicit knowledge injection, showing that skills stabilize action rather than inject missing facts." (p.1, abstract)
- "exact ground-truth skill invocation is neither sufficient nor strictly necessary for success." (p.10, section 5.5)
- Implementation detail: skills were "placed in the execution environment as reusable procedural resources rather than fully incorporated into the initial context" (p.6). The paper does not test progressive disclosure as a variable.

LIMITS (authors and my reading)
- Only terminal and tool-using benchmarks, and only a few agent-model pairings. Authors concede findings may not generalise to other scaffolds, model families or versions.
- The taxonomy comes from open coding of 240 trajectories, about 3% of the records. Rare modes may be missed.
- The 528 triples are labelled by an LLM judge. Only the taxonomy construction was human-validated (Cohen's κ = 0.952, 95.8% exact agreement on 238 labels).
- Skills here are auto-distilled from agent trajectories by an LLM prompt (Appendix B.1). They are not human-authored or curated Anthropic-style skills.
- The gain over raw is not statistically significant. Significance holds only against workflow memory.
- RQ4 used GPT-5.4, while RQ1-RQ3 used GPT-5.3-Codex, so RQ4 cannot be compared with them in absolute terms.
- Token data is incomplete for some skill runs. The paper does not test frontmatter-only versus full-body loading, or description quality.
- Terminal-Bench-Pro counts infrastructure and verifier errors as failures.

BUILDS ON
- Anthropic 2025 (Skills repository).
- Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2024c).
- Memp (Fang et al. 2026).
- SkillsBench (Li et al. 2026).
- SWE-Skills-Bench (Han et al. 2026).
- Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al. 2026).
- Harbor (2026).
- Trace2Skill (Ni et al. 2026).
- Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023).
- Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023).
- MemGPT (Packer et al. 2024).
- Qwen3-Embedding (Zhang et al. 2025).
